```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

## Objective

Explore the distribution of weekly lunch frequency by self-reported gender. This is a descriptive comparison, not an analysis of causal effects.

## Load and validate

```{r load-and-validate}
input_path <- "survey_data.csv"
if (!file.exists(input_path)) stop("A locally authorised survey_data.csv is required.")
diet <- read.csv(input_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(all(c("Lunch", "Gender") %in% names(diet)))
stopifnot(is.numeric(diet$Lunch), !anyNA(diet$Lunch))
stopifnot(all(diet$Lunch %in% 0:7), all(diet$Lunch == as.integer(diet$Lunch)))
stopifnot(!anyNA(diet$Gender), all(nzchar(trimws(diet$Gender))))
analysis <- data.frame(
  days = factor(diet$Lunch, levels = 0:7),
  gender = factor(diet$Gender)
)
cat("Respondents:", nrow(analysis), "\n")
cat("Source variables:", ncol(diet), "\n")
cat("Missing values in analysis:", sum(is.na(analysis)), "\n")
```

## Visualisation

This single stacked bar chart displays respondent counts by lunch frequency and gender.

```{r lunch-chart, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.8, dpi=140, fig.align='center', fig.cap='Weekly lunch frequency by gender (respondent counts).'}
library(ggplot2)
lunch_chart <- ggplot(analysis, aes(x = days, fill = gender)) +
  geom_bar(width = 0.8) +
  scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Lunch Frequency by Gender",
       x = "Days per week", y = "Respondents (count)",
       fill = "Gender") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
lunch_chart
```

## Descriptive summary

```{r summary}
frequency <- as.integer(table(factor(diet$Lunch, levels = 0:7)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Days_per_week = 0:7, Respondents = frequency))
cat("Reporting lunch every day:", frequency[8], "of", nrow(diet),
    sprintf("(%.1f%%)", 100 * frequency[8] / nrow(diet)), "\n")
```

## Limitations

Gender groups are imbalanced in this sample. One category has only one respondent; avoid population-level interpretations or comparisons based on that group. No causal claims can be made from these cross-sectional self-reports.

The respondent-level dataset is intentionally kept out of the public repository.
